newsitem.title: USA: U.S., EU harmonize, but not in tune on ag issues.
newsitem.headline: U.S., EU harmonize, but not in tune on ag issues.

text.p: The two top U.S. and European Union policymakers for agriculture disagreed on several major issues Monday but nonetheless declared their twice-a-year meetings soothed transatlantic tensions.

They announced some progress in a dispute that has stalled U.S.-EU poultry trade for the past two months. A U.S. Agriculture Department team will assess EU slaughter and inspection methods but no date was set.
"Yes, I would say we have moved it forward some," Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman told reporters, adding, "We have not changed the (overall meat inspection) agreement."

While Glickman and his EU counterpart, Franz Fischler, listed several areas of disagreement, covering hundreds of milions of dollars in trade, they spent as much time saying that regular meetings were the foundation of progress.
"We had a long list of issues to discuss," Fischler said. "We are making progress...We are solving problems."

A dominant issue in the 75 minutes of talks before a lunch break was genetically engineered crops. Europe is far more skeptical than the United States of the crops and is studying the idea of requiring special labels on them and foods made with them.
U.S. officials told Fischler they believe separate handling of biotech crops, an idea put forward by some consumer groups, was unneeded and prohibitively expensive for safe products.
"We talked in great detail on the GMO (genetically modified organism) issue," Glickman said.
Fischler said it was important to recognize and understand the cultural differences between the two markets.

The two leaders briefly discussed the "hormone beef" dispute in the context of consumer attitudes toward meat production techniques. A World Trade Organization panel has ruled a decade-old EU ban on imports of U.S. beef produced with synthetic growth hormones was unjustified. The EU was expected to appeal the ruling when it becomes final in the summer.
A wine pact, spelling out nomenclature that can be used by vintners -- for example, who can claim to produce champagne -- might be reached by fall, Fischler said.
No agreement was reached on access for U.S. rice to the EU market.

Earlier in the day, Fischler signaled EU intention to remain one of the world's major agricultural trading powers for years to come. Revision of the EU's Common Agricultural Policy must let farmers seek a profit in the marketplace and rely less on price supports or artificially high prices, he said.

"With their high quality standards, our agricultural and food products have already demonstrated their ability to compete successfully on the world market," he said in a speech to the European Institute, a think tank.
